The novel psychoactive substance (NPS) phenomenon represents a major global problem. Despite the methodical inclusion of new analogues in lists of controlled drugs, new compounds continue to circulate, frequently resulting in fatal intoxications. The emergence of N-isopropyl butylone (NiPB) in 2024, found as an adulterant in methamphetamine-based products, underscores the rapidly evolving landscape of NPSs. Despite its structural similarity to potent monoamine transporter inhibitors, specific pharmacological data and information on its effects in consumers are currently lacking. This study aims to characterize the acute physiological, behavioural, and sensorimotor effects of NiPB (0.1–60 mg/kg; i.p.) in male mice, complemented by in silico pharmacokinetic modelling (ADMET Predictor®). NiPB is predicted to undergo N-dealkylation, cleavage of the 3,4-methylendioxy moiety, and N-glucuronidation. Computational profiling predicted high BBB permeability, Vd = 4.37 L/kg, fup > 50%, CYP2D6 and OCT2 inhibition, and hERG blockade (pIC50 = 4.888). In vivo, NiPB induced dose-dependent locomotor stimulation without affecting motor coordination and provoked tachypnoea and visual reflex alterations, while tactile and acoustic responses, as well as thermoregulation, were preserved. In conclusion, this study defines the preliminary toxicological profile of NiPB, indicating that acute exposure may trigger central psychostimulant toxicity in vivo. Furthermore, based on the in silico profiling, targeted experimental studies are required to determine the actual cardiotoxicity and risks of drug–drug interactions associated with NiPB.

1. Introduction

Synthetic cathinones are part of the ever-increasing and constantly evolving group of novel psychoactive substances (NPSs)—drugs developed to circumvent legal restrictions on traditional drugs of abuse. The common mechanism of action of synthetic cathinones involves increasing synaptic concentrations of monoamines through interactions with reuptake transporters, triggering effects similar to those of cocaine or amphetamine, such as euphoria, increased sociability, increased energy, reduced fatigue, and intensification of sensory experiences. Conversely, consumers and case reports describe side effects including agitation and aggressiveness, paranoia, psychosis, and hallucinations, alongside cardiovascular complications (tachycardia, thoracic pain, hypertension, cardiac arrest), respiratory distress, hyperthermia, nausea, and vomiting [1].

The emergence and abuse of novel cathinone derivatives have surged in recent years. Worldwide, 228 synthetic cathinones have been reported, with 115 compounds identified between 2024 and 2025 [2]. In 2024, seven new derivatives were first discovered in Europe [3]. In the same year, a novel compound, N-isopropylbutylone (NiPB; Figure 1), was identified alongside methamphetamine in a drug material [4]. This compound has also been found in ecstasy tablets along with methamphetamine and ketamine [5], while its seizure by Italian Authorities was reported in 2025. Structurally, NiPB is closely related to butylone and eutylone (Figure 1), two hybrid transporter compounds that inhibit DAT and NET while possessing substrate-type releasing effects at SERT [6].

In particular, NiPB shares the same 3,4-methylenedioxy ring substitution and α-carbon side chain with eutylone and butylone. Starting from the structure of butylone, the N-alkyl moiety has been sequentially expanded from an N-methyl group (butylone) to an N-ethyl group (eutylone) and then to an N-isopropyl group (NiPB). The increase in the size and bulkiness of the substituent at the amine group is generally associated with an enhanced potency of inhibition at DAT and a significant increase in the DAT/SERT ratio [7]. In line with this, in vitro studies show that butylone and eutylone differ in their DAT inhibitory potency, with reported IC50 values of 1710 ± 320 nM and 120 ± 10 nM, respectively [6,8]. Based on these SAR principles, we hypothesized that the bulky N-isopropyl substitution in NiPB further reinforces DAT inhibitory potency and DAT/SERT selectivity, resulting in a predominantly dopaminergic psychostimulant profile in vivo.

Although a monograph on NiPB was published by the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education [4], data regarding its pharmacological profile and effects in animals or humans remain scarce. To address this critical knowledge gap, our study aims to provide a preliminary evaluation of the pharmaco-toxicological profile of NiPB. In particular, we conducted tests on its ADMET profile using the in silico ADMET Predictor® 14.0 (x64) software and evaluated its acute effects in mice. As a Collaborative Centre of the Department of Anti-Drug Policies (DPA), Presidency of the Council of Ministers (PCM), our objective is to provide relevant toxicological and clinical data to assist forensic experts and clinicians in the management of potential NiPB intoxication cases and to pre-empt a potential health risk associated with the circulation of this compound.

2. Results

2.1. Predicted Metabolic Pathway

Based on ADMET Predictor®, NiPB is estimated to be a substrate of CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP2D6 (Figure 2).

In particular, these enzymes were predicted to promote (i) hydroxylation at the N-isopropyl function and consequently N-dealkylation; (ii) hydroxylation at the 3,4-methylenedioxy moiety, followed by the opening of the ring and production of the 3,4-catechol metabolite, which is predicted to undergo oxidation at the hydroxyl groups. Moreover, UGT1A4 and UGT2B7 were predicted to take part in the metabolism of NiPB, which would produce the N-glucuronic metabolite (Figure 2).

2.2. Predicted ADMET Properties

Table 1 shows the predicted inhibition of cytochrome enzymes by NiPB. Among all the tested CYPs, the compound was predicted to inhibit CYP2D6.

ADMET Predictor® calculated a high penetrance of the blood–brain barrier (BBB; Table 2). NiPB was not predicted to be a substrate or an inhibitor of P-glycoprotein (PgP) and organic cation transporter 1 (OCT1). In contrast, the compound was estimated to be both a substrate and an inhibitor of organic cation transporter 2 (OCT2). The software predicted a good percentage of compound unbound to blood plasma proteins (>50%) in both humans (hum_fup) and mice (mou_fup), and a high volume of distribution at steady state (>3.7 L/kg). Finally, NiPB was not predicted to inhibit BSEP, as the calculated IC50 (BSEP_IC50) value exceeded the threshold of 60 μM.

The toxic potential of NiPB is shown in Table 3. The compound was not predicted to induce alterations in the serum levels of alkaline phosphatase (Ser_AlkPhos), gamma-glutamyl transferase (Ser_GGT), lactate dehydrogenase (Ser_LDH), aspartic acid transaminase (Ser_AST), or alanine transaminase (Ser_ALT). Furthermore, the compound was not predicted to exhibit androgen (Andro_Filter) or estrogen (Estro_Filter) receptor toxicity in rats. Instead, it was predicted to cause respiratory allergenic sensitization in rats (Sens_Resp) and to block the potassium channel in humans (hERG_Filter), with a calculated pIC50 of 4.888.

2.3. Acute Effects in Mice

2.3.1. Physiological Parameters

Systemic injection of the lowest dose of NiPB (0.1 mg/kg) did not induce significant effects in male mice. In contrast, a transient increase in respiration rate was observed at doses of 1 mg/kg (only at 5 min post-administration), 10 mg/kg (until 30 min post-administration), 30 mg/kg (at 5 min and again between 60 and 120 min post-administration), and 60 mg/kg (until 120 min post-treatment) [Figure 3A; two-way RM ANOVA, main effect of treatment: F(5, 30) = 5.131 and p = 0.0016; time: F(7, 210) = 11.02 and p < 0.0001; treatment × time interaction: F(35, 210) = 2.628 and p < 0.0001].

Notably, none of the tested doses of NiPB altered the core body temperature of the mice (Figure 3B).

2.3.2. Sensorial Responses

NiPB induced a significant reduction in the visual placing reflex in male mice. Specifically, the 1 mg/kg dose induced a transient effect, while higher doses (10–60 mg/kg) led to more profound and prolonged impairment [Figure 4A; two-way RM ANOVA, main effect of treatment: F(5, 30) = 114.5 and p < 0.0001, time: F(7, 210) = 60.91 and p < 0.0001, treatment × time interaction: F(35, 210) = 9.155 and p < 0.0001].

However, NiPB (0.1–60 mg/kg) did not affect visual object (Figure 4B), acoustic (Figure 4C), or tactile responses (Figure 4D).

2.3.3. Locomotory Activity

Treatment with NiPB (1–60 mg/kg) induced a dose-dependent increase in spontaneous locomotory activity. Specifically, the 1 and 10 mg/kg doses caused significant effects only during the first 5 and 30 min, respectively. The 30 mg/kg dose increased activity during the first hour and again at 300 min. The highest dose tested induced a persistent stimulatory effect [Figure 5A; two-way RM ANOVA, main effect of treatment: F(5, 30) = 21.74 and p < 0.0001, time: F(7, 210) = 49.66 and p < 0.0001, treatment × time interaction: F(35, 210) = 6.027 and p < 0.0001].

Finally, the compound did not induce motor impairments or affect performance in the rotarod test (Figure 5B).

3. Discussion

The present work provides novel information on a recently identified synthetic cathinone, i.e., NiPB. Given the absence of data on its pharmacokinetic characteristics and its pharmaco-toxicological effects, we evaluated its ADMET properties and its acute effects in male CD-1 mice.

The in silico analysis revealed a metabolic profile consistent with previous computational, in vitro, and in vivo studies on related cathinones [9,10,11,12,13,14]. Indeed, NiPB was predicted to undergo N-dealkylation, producing a metabolite shared with butylone and N-propylbutylone. A second predicted metabolite results from cleavage of the 3,4-methylendioxy moiety. These reactions were predicted to be mediated by CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP2D6. Furthermore, in silico modelling suggested a potential for CYP2D6 inhibition, although this output was generated with moderate prediction confidence (accuracy of 58%), representing a hypothetical risk for pharmacokinetic drug–drug interactions that requires experimental validation. While future studies are needed to confirm these pathways, khat has been reported to inhibit CYP2D6 in humans [15], and an in vitro study demonstrated the ability of methylenedioxy-derived designer drugs, butylone and MDPV, to inhibit this isoform [16]. Furthermore, eutylone was recently shown to be metabolized by CYP2D6, CYP2C19, and CYP2B6 while inducing a time-dependent inhibition of CYP2D6 [17]. Finally, the software predicted phase II N-glucuronidation by UGT1A4 and UGT2B7. Although information regarding phase II metabolites of synthetic cathinones remains limited, glucuronide conjugates have been identified for both eutylone and mephedrone [11,17,18].

Based on our analysis, NiPB exhibits high predicted permeability across the BBB. Additionally, the software suggested a potential interaction with OCT2 as both a substrate and an inhibitor, albeit with modest prediction confidence (accuracies of 67% and 55%, respectively). Given the pivotal role of this transporter in the renal secretion of organic cations [19], this result suggests a theoretical risk for drug–drug interactions that warrants experimental validation. Our computational profiling yielded a predicted human Vd of 4.371 L/kg (slightly above the threshold of 3.7 L/kg), along with a high fraction of compound unbound to plasma proteins (>50%). These parameters are closely interconnected [20]: while the high unbound fraction suggests that a major portion of circulating NiPB potentially remains available for biological interaction, the Vd value points towards a possible propensity for extravascular tissue redistribution in humans, without necessarily implying excessive tissue sequestration. The Vd of synthetic cathinones is a PK parameter influenced by multiple factors, including chemical structure, chirality, dose, and biological sex. For instance, methylone and butylone exhibit greater tissue distribution than pentylone [21], whereas the Vd of MDPV enantiomers shows sex-dependent variations [22]. Furthermore, alpha-PVP has also been reported to possess a high Vd in male rats, highlighting how structural modifications across this substance class affect tissue partitioning profiles [23].

We also evaluated the potential inhibition of BSEP, a crucial hepatic transporter, whose blockade is closely linked to drug-induced liver injury [24]. Similar to MDPV and MDPHP [10], NiPB was not predicted to inhibit BSEP. Furthermore, computational modelling disclosed that NiPB lacks significant propensity for human hepatotoxicity or androgen- or estrogen receptor-mediated toxicity in rat models. Nevertheless, in light of its predicted Vd and potential for tissue redistribution, these toxicological profiles warrant experimental validation in animal models. Indeed, tissue retention and redistribution of drugs of abuse can prolong systemic effects via gradual release back into the bloodstream or induce localized organ toxicity [20]. This is particularly relevant given that synthetic cathinones are frequently associated with multi-organ toxicities, including rhabdomyolysis, hepatotoxicity, and cardiotoxicity [25,26,27,28,29,30]. Finally, NiPB was predicted to act as a respiratory sensitizer. Since synthetic cathinones are commonly administered via the nasal route, their potential to trigger airway hypersensitivity represents a clinically relevant feature [31].

Notably, the compound was predicted to interact with the human hERG potassium channel (pIC50 of 4.888, corresponding to an IC50 of approximately 12.9 μM), indicating a potential risk of QT-interval prolongation and fatal arrhythmias, such as torsades de pointes [32]. In absolute terms, this micromolar affinity indicates a low intrinsic blocking potency at the hERG channel [33]. However, this risk must be contextualized with systemic exposure and free plasma concentrations [34]. While high-dose regimens (up to 60 mg/kg) were evaluated in our behavioural protocol and computational ADMET profiling predicted an unbound fraction exceeding 50%, no systemic pharmacokinetic (PK) data are currently available to measure actual free plasma concentrations in vivo. Therefore, this finding requires experimental confirmation, including dedicated PK evaluations and functional electrophysiological assays, in order to establish the true cardiac safety margin. Cardiotoxicity is among the most frequently reported symptoms of synthetic cathinone intoxications [35], and previous studies have focused on the effects of synthetic cathinones on cardiac function. For example, MDPV was found to induce ventricular bradycardia and AV block in zebrafish model [36] and to prolong the field potential duration in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes [35], which highlights an association between MDPV and QT prolongation. Another example is represented by the atypical synthetic cathinone 4,4′-DMAR, which has recently been demonstrated to induce QT-interval prolongation in male mice [37]. On this basis, future research must prioritize the evaluation of NiPB effects on cardiovascular and cardiomyocyte functions.

As previously mentioned, the circulation of NiPB on the NPS market has only recently been reported; hence, this is the first study to describe its pharmacological effects in mice. Given its chemical structure, NiPB was expected to induce behavioural, physiological, and sensorimotor profiles similar to those previously observed with other synthetic cathinones, particularly 3,4-methylenedioxy derivatives (e.g., eutylone, butylone, MDPV, MDPHP, N-ethylpentylone, dimethylone, and dibutylone) [6,8,10,38]. In accordance with this hypothesis, NiPB induced dose-dependent locomotor stimulation and transient tachypnoea while inhibiting the visual placing response, which points toward an alteration in proprioceptive reflex control. The compound did not affect other sensorimotor responses or motor coordination. This contrasts with other psychoactive substances associated with disrupted acoustic or tactile reactivity, such as NM2AI or MTTA [39,40], or with marked stereotypies and postural instability, such as MDPV, 3-FMC, 4-FMC, or 3-CMC [10,25,41]. Furthermore, NiPB did not alter thermoregulation in mice. While this differs from the hyperthermic responses frequently reported following cathinone consumption in humans [42], it aligns with the modest, if any, effects on rodent body temperature observed with several related compounds [43,44].

Based on previous observations with related synthetic cathinones, we anticipated significant locomotor stimulation even at low doses of NiPB. For instance, Glatfelter and colleagues [6] showed that eutylone produces significant hyperlocomotion in male C57BL/6J mice at a dose of 3 mg/kg (s.c.). Similarly, our previous work [10] with CD-1 mice demonstrated that MDPV increases the total distance travelled at 1 mg/kg (i.p.). In contrast, NiPB exhibited lower in vivo potency, as significant locomotor activation was observed only at higher doses (10–60 mg/kg). From a structure–activity relationship (SAR) perspective [7], we initially hypothesized that NiPB would possess higher dopamine transporter (DAT) inhibitory potency than eutylone, ultimately producing greater locomotor activation. However, Glatfelter et al. (2021) demonstrated that, despite differences in α-carbon and amine side-chain substituents, eutylone, pentylone, and dibutylone display comparable DAT interactions while exhibiting distinct potencies in stimulating locomotion [6]. This underscores that in vitro SAR data do not always directly correlate with in vivo behavioural outcomes. Nevertheless, our findings demonstrate for the first time that NiPB acts as a psychostimulant, aligning with the general profile of synthetic cathinones.

Because direct in vitro binding or functional assays of monoamine transporters were not performed in the present study, the exact neurochemical mechanism underlying the actions of NiPB remains to be established. Nevertheless, the observed behavioural and physiological responses are broadly consistent with monoaminergic activation. In particular, central noradrenergic pathways are known to regulate respiratory rhythm via α-adrenergic receptors in the brainstem [45,46,47] and to modulate sensorimotor reflex integration such as vestibulo-ocular and optokinetic responses [48], providing a plausible functional context for the observed tachypnoea and visual placing impairment. This observation aligns with reported data for eutylone and butylone, which display NET inhibitory potencies of 1280 ± 140 nM and 920 ± 130 nM, respectively [6,8]. Similarly, dose-dependent hyperlocomotion represents a characteristic behavioural signature often associated with increased synaptic DA levels in the ventral striatum [7], consistent with the known effects of reference cathinones and other psychostimulants [49,50,51]. Regarding central nervous system (CNS) accessibility, the observed dose-dependent behavioural effects support central activity and are consistent with the in silico predictions of high BBB permeability.

Finally, related cathinones such as eutylone (IC50 = 690 ± 50 nM and EC50 = 1020 ± 260 nM) and butylone (IC50 = 680 ± 130 nM) [6,8] display SERT activity, which in vivo is frequently associated with hyperthermia and disruptions of tactile or acoustic reflexes, as described for serotonergic psychostimulants like MTTA, NM2AI, or 4,4′-DMAR [39,40,52]. In our study, the tested dose range of NiPB failed to induce these characteristic serotoninergic signs. However, the absence of these manifestations cannot be interpreted as proof of DAT/SERT selectivity of preferential dopaminergic/noradrenergic activation. Direct in vitro binding and functional reuptake/release assays remain strictly necessary to definitively characterize the target affinity, selectivity profile, and transporter interactions of NiPB.

4. Materials and Methods

4.1. ADMET Prediction

Simulation Plus ADMET Predictor® Version 10.4 (x64) on a Windows 11 operating system (ADMET Predictor® 14.0, Simulations-Plus Inc., Durham, NC, USA) was employed to predict the ADMET profile of NiPB. As mentioned in previous studies [10,25,53], this cheminformatics platform utilizes Quantitative Structure–Activity/Property Relationship (QSAR/QSPR) machine learning models, primarily Artificial Neural Network Ensembles (ANNE), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Kernel Partial Least Squares (KPLS), trained on curated experimental datasets of well-defined drugs using 2D molecular structures and atomic descriptors. Unlike platforms relying on static literature lookup tables or basic web utilities, ADMET Predictor® employs ensemble architectures to maintain predictive performance when applied to novel chemical structures. Model robustness and generalizability are ensured by partitioning datasets into training, verification, and external test sets (via Kohonen self-organizing maps or stratified sampling) alongside early stopping protocols to prevent overtraining. Predictive performance is validated using held-out external test sets assessed using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and R2 for continuous properties, as well as Concordance (accuracy), Sensitivity, and Specificity for classification models. In independent comparative evaluations, ADMET Predictor®’s physicochemical models (e.g., S + logP and S + Sw) have demonstrated superior or comparable performance relative to other widely used prediction platforms (e.g., Dragon) and established literature QSAR models. Furthermore, to prevent overconfident extrapolation, all predictions incorporate defined applicability domain assessments and generate compound-specific confidence metrics.

4.2. Animals

Thirty-six adult male ICR (CD-1®) mice (3–4 months old, weighing 25–30 g; ENVIGO Harlan Italy, Ferrara, Italy; bred inside the Laboratory for Preclinical Research (LARP) of University of Ferrara, Italy), were group-housed (5 mice per cage; a floor area per animal of 80 cm2; a minimum enclosure height of 12 cm). Animals were exposed to a 12:12-h light–dark cycle at a temperature of 20–22 °C and humidity of 45–55%, with ad libitum access to food (Diet 4RF25 GLP; Mucedola, Settimo Milanese, Milan, Italy) and water. The experimental protocols followed in the present study were in accordance with the U.K. Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act of 1986 and associated guidelines and the new European Communities Council Directive of September 2010 (2010/63/EU). The Italian Ministry of Health (license no. 1168/2024-PR, CBCC2.79.EXT.44) and the Animal Welfare Body of the University of Ferrara approved experimental protocols. According to the ARRIVE guidelines, all possible efforts were made to minimize the number of animals used and the animals’ pain and discomfort. For the present study, 6 mice were employed for each treatment (vehicle or 5 different doses of NiPB, 0.1–60 mg/kg). An a priori power analysis was performed using G*Power 3.1 [54] to determine the total sample size for the behavioural testing protocol. Based on the expected dose-dependent pharmacological profiles (effect size f calculated according to Cohen, 1988 [55]), a significance level of α = 0.05, and a statistical power of 1–β = 0.80, a sample size of 6 animals per group was calculated to be sufficient to detect an effect size of 0.50 for the primary behavioural endpoint (tactile reflex). The GraphPad calculator [56] was employed to randomly assign subjects to treatment groups. We randomly assigned a total of 6 subjects to each of the 6 groups.

4.3. Drug Preparation and Dose Selection

N-isopropylbutylone hydrochloride was purchased from LGC Standards S.r.l. (Milan, Italy). The compound was dissolved in saline solution (0.9% NaCl), which was also employed as the vehicle. The drug was administered via intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection at a volume of 4 µL/g. The doses of the tested compound were chosen based on previous studies conducted with synthetic cathinones (MDPV and MDPHP) and a cathinone-like compound (MTTA) [10,39].

4.4. Behavioural Studies

For the present study, the effects of systemic administration of NiPB at different doses on behavioural responses were investigated as previously described [25,40] using a battery of tests largely employed in our laboratory for Safety Pharmacology studies in a murine model [57]. The protocol was designed to minimize the number of mice employed and consisted of consecutive functional observational tests, according to the following scheme: respiratory rate, spontaneous locomotion, sensorimotor (visual placing, visual object, acoustic, and overall tactile) reflexes, rectal temperature, and stimulated motor activity. The battery of tests was conducted at 0 (basal values), 5, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240, and 300 min after treatment with vehicle or NiPB (0.1–60 mg/kg). During the experiment, mice were individually housed in an experimental chamber (350 mm × 350 mm × 350 mm) with black methacrylate walls and a transparent front door. The randomized assignment of each subject to a treatment group (see Section 4.2) and the drug preparation (see Section 4.3) were conducted by a single operator, while behavioural observations were conducted by different trained operators working in pairs who were not aware of the treatment.

4.4.1. Respiratory Rate

To assess respiratory rate, mice were placed in individual cages and allowed to move freely [25]. An operator analyzed video footage of the mice’s videotaped respiration patterns offline and counted the number of the animal’s thoracic extensions within a minute.

4.4.2. Mobility Time

The mobility time test involved allowing the animal to move freely in a square plastic cage (60 cm × 60 cm) and using a stopwatch to measure the total time the animal remained in motion over a period of 300 s (5 min) [40]. Mouse activity was recorded using one camera (B/W USB day and night with varifocal, Ugo Basile, Ferrara, Italy), and the recordings were analyzed offline in a blind manner by a different operator.

4.4.3. Visual Responses

To evaluate the ability of the animal to capture visual information, two different tests were performed: one when the animal was stationary (visual object) and the other when the animal was moving (visual placing) [40].

The visual placing test was performed using a modified tail-suspension apparatus that brought the mouse toward the floor at a constant speed of 10 cm/sec. Analysis of the video frames made it possible to evaluate the start of the mouse’s reaction as it approached the floor. Mice typically respond by extending the front paws, and an electronic ruler measures the perpendicular distance (mm) from the floor at which the mouse starts the reaction.

The visual object test was performed to evaluate the mice’s ability to respond to the sight of an approaching object presented from the front (using a white horizontal bar) or from the side (using a small dentist’s mirror). A score of 1 was assigned if the mouse showed a response to the stimulus, and a score of 0 if no response was observed. Mice usually respond by turning their head or retracting. For the frontal visual response, the bar was moved toward the front of the mouse’s head 3 times. For the lateral visual response, the procedure was conducted bilaterally and repeated 3 times. The total score was calculated by summing the scores obtained from each test (overall score: 9).

4.4.4. Acoustic Responses

In the acoustic test, four different stimuli (varying in intensity and frequency) were presented behind the animal, and the reflex response of the mouse was recorded by the operator [25]. Each stimulus was repeated 3 times, with a score of 1 in the presence of a reflex or 0 if absent. The total score was calculated by summing the scores obtained from each test (overall score: 12).

4.4.5. Tactile Responses

The tactile responses of mice were assessed through vibrissae, corneal, and pinnae reflexes [40] using a gavage needle, with a score of 1 in the presence of a response or 0 if absent. Reflexes were assessed by gently touching the vibrissae (right and left, once per side), the cornea (right and left, 3 times per side), and pinnae (left and right, 2 times per side). Data are expressed as the sum of the three parameters (overall score: 12).

4.4.6. Body Temperature

Core temperature was evaluated using a probe (1 mm diameter) connected to a Cole–Parmer digital thermometer (model 8402; Vernon Hills, IL, USA). After lubrication with liquid vaseline, the probe was gently inserted into the rectum of the mouse (to a depth of approximately 2 cm) and left in position until the temperature stabilized (approximately 10 s) [25].

4.4.7. Rotarod

The accelerod test was used to assess alterations in stimulated motor activity induced by NiPB [25]. Mice were placed on the rotarod, which consists of a rotating cylinder that constantly increases its rotation speed (0–60 rotations/min over 5 min). The time for which mice could stand on the rotarod during a period of 300 s was measured using a stopwatch.

4.5. Data and Statistical Analysis

Data are represented as % of basal values (respiratory rate, visual placing response, mobility time, and rotarod), as Δ°C relative to basal values (rectal temperature), and as arbitrary units (visual object, acoustic, and overall tactile responses). All data are shown as mean ± SEM from 6 independent experimental replications. The Shapiro–Wilk test was used to establish and confirm the normality of the parameters. Two-way RM ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s test for multiple comparisons was employed for the statistical analysis of the effects of NiPB (0.1–60 mg/kg; i.p.) over time. All statistical analyses were performed using Prism 8.0 software (GraphPad Prism, San Diego, CA, USA). Results were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05 (solid symbol) versus vehicle.

5. Conclusions and Real-World Implications

The present work addresses a critical gap in the literature regarding NiPB, a novel synthetic cathinone that, although not yet associated with documented clinical intoxication, poses an emerging threat as illicit markets adapt to legislative restrictions on structural predecessors [58]. Identifying new compounds and establishing appropriate diagnostic methods, clinical management, and treatment protocols for cases of novel psychoactive substance (NPS)-related intoxication remains a significant challenge [59].

Although limited to acute observations in male mice and computational modelling, our findings offer preliminary insights into the potential risk profile of NiPB, particularly in scenarios involving acute overdose or polydrug use. The in silico ADMET profiling predicted potential hERG channel blockage, generating a theoretical hypothesis regarding cardiotoxicity. While cardiovascular symptoms such as tachycardia, palpitations, and chest pain, potentially escalating to cardiac arrest, myocardial infarction, and life-threatening arrhythmias, are well documented for the cathinone-containing plant khat [60] and related synthetic cathinones [61,62,63], dedicated assays and exposure measurements are required to evaluate whether NiPB exerts direct cardiotoxic effects in vivo.

Another critical aspect emerging from clinical case reports is the occurrence of severe agitation, aggressiveness, and acute psychosis among synthetic cathinone users [25,61,62,64]. From a translational perspective, drug-induced hyperlocomotion in rodents provides a preclinical parallel to psychomotor agitation. This characteristic response to acute synthetic cathinone intoxication [41] presents a major challenge in emergency settings, as severe agitation hampers patient management and clinical examination and complicates the collection of information regarding the ingested substance and dosage. In this regard, the dose-dependent hyperlocomotion observed in mice after treatment with NiPB suggests that the compound could potentially be associated with similar behavioural manifestations following acute exposure.

Synthetic cathinones are frequently co-consumed with other illicit substances, including alcohol, cannabis, and stimulant-like compounds [65], as well as sedatives and opioids [66,67]. Moreover, users are often unaware of multi-substance exposure, as commercial “bath salt” products frequently contain undisclosed mixtures, and NPS may be added as adulterants or cutting agents [66,68,69]. Our in silico evaluation suggests that NiPB might inhibit CYP2D6 and OCT2, generating a preliminary hypothesis regarding drug–drug interactions. If experimentally validated, such inhibition could alter the clearance of co-administered substances, potentially increasing the risk of systemic toxicity.

Finally, while human biotransformation profiles remain to be fully characterized, recent in vivo evidence in mice [70] supports the predicted metabolic pathways, offering a baseline for analytical screening protocols in forensic and clinical toxicology. In this framework, integrating computational ADMET profiling with in vivo screening offers a rapid, cost-effective, and ethically sound strategy to proactively characterize newly emerging NPS before widespread clinical presentation occurs.

6. Limitations

Several methodological limitations of the present study should be noted. While computational modelling successfully predicted central penetration, in silico predictions require full in vitro and in vivo validation. Specifically, formal radioligand-binding and functional transporter assays are needed to definitively quantify the affinity and selectivity of NiPB at DAT, NET, and SERT. The absence of systemic PK measurements in the present study precludes a direct correlation between circulating plasma exposure and the observed behavioural or physiological effects. Moreover, in vivo testing was restricted to male subjects, a choice aligned with the higher epidemiological prevalence of synthetic cathinone use among males [71]. However, given that synthetic cathinones are also consumed by females [72] and that sex can markedly influence psychostimulant pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics [25,44,73,74,75], future investigations should prioritize evaluating sex-tailored responses, full internal PK profiling, and direct electrophysiological assessments of cardiac safety.

Abstract

Background

Inadvertent perioperative hypothermia is associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes, but adequately powered trials using high-sensitivity troponin endpoints is lacking. The SAGE trial evaluates whether an intelligent, closed-loop thermoregulation strategy reduces myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS) in high-risk elderly patients.

Methods

This prospective, multicenter, parallel-group, randomized controlled superiority trial conducted at seven tertiary hospitals in China. Participants aged ≥65 years scheduled for elective gastrointestinal tumor resection under general anesthesia are randomly assigned (1:1) to intelligent closed-loop warming (target 36.8 °C, upper limit 37.0 °C) or routine thermal management (active warming only if core temperature ≤35.5 °C). The primary outcome is the incidence of MINS within the first 2 postoperative days , adjudicated using high-sensitivity troponin thresholds per AHA criteria. Secondary outcomes include surgical site infection, transfusion requirement, hypothermia burden, emergence delirium, delayed emergence, and postoperative shivering. With 695 participants per group (total 1,390, accounting for 10% dropout), the trial has 80% power at a one-sided significance level of 0.05 to detect a 6 absolute percentage point reduction in MINS (12% to 6%) with a superiority margin of −2 percentage points.

Discussion

The SAGE trial is designed to generate new evidence on the relationship between intraoperative hypothermia exposure and postoperative cardiovascular complications. It will evaluate whether closed-loop targeted normothermia reduces myocardial injury and will explore hypothermia exposure thresholds that may inform individualized perioperative management for geriatric surgical patients.

Trial Acronym

Intelligent Thermoregulation Strategy for Advanced-Age Elders undergoing gastrointestinal tumor resection (SAGE).

Trial Registration

Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR), identifier: ChiCTR2600117264. Registered on January 21, 2026 (http://www.chictr.org.cn).

Introduction

Background and rationale

While perioperative mortality has declined substantially over recent decades, postoperative mortality remains a significant global health burden. Approximately 1%–2% of surgical inpatients die within 30 days of surgery, with cardiovascular complications constituting the leading cause of postoperative death [1,2]. Myocardial injury, defined by postoperative troponin elevation attributable to an ischemic etiology, is the most prevalent of these cardiovascular complications. It is now recognized that approximately 8% of surgical inpatients aged >45 years’ experience Myocardial Injury after Noncardiac Surgery (MINS), yet the majority of these events are clinically silent and would remain undetected without systematic troponin surveillance[3,4]. Critically, MINS is not a benign biochemical anomaly; it confers a five-fold increase in 30-day mortality, with risk escalating exponentially as a function of peak troponin concentration [4,5]. Consequently, identification of modifiable perioperative risk factors for MINS is a clinical and research priority.

Inadvertent perioperative hypothermia (IPH), defined as a core body temperature < 36.0 °C, is one such potentially modifiable factor. IPH occurs with a reported incidence ranging from 7% to 90% [6–8], with nationwide surveys in China documenting rates of 39.9% in Beijing [9] and 44.5% across multiple regions [10]. Hypothermia triggers thermoregulatory vasoconstriction, elevating systemic vascular resistance and inducing tachycardia, mechanisms which may precipitate myocardial oxygen supply-demand mismatch [11]. Observational data link IPH to a higher incidence of perioperative cardiovascular events; specifically, normothermic patients exhibit a 1.4% event rate compared to 6.3% in hypothermic cohorts, with corresponding increases in ventricular arrhythmias and myocardial ischemia [12,13]. Beyond cardiovascular sequelae, IPH is associated with coagulopathy, increased transfusion requirements, surgical site infection (19% vs. 6% in normothermic patients), and prolonged hospitalization [14–17].

Despite these associations, the causal link between aggressive normothermia and reduction in major adverse cardiac events remains incompletely defined. A pivotal randomized trial by Frank et al. [12] suggested a cardioprotective signal with active warming; however, the study was of relatively modest sample size and, as conducted before the widespread adoption of high-sensitivity troponin assays, relied on Holter electrocardiography for outcome ascertainment. This diagnostic approach, while appropriate to its era, is substantially less sensitive for detecting perioperative myocardial injury than contemporary biomarker-based definitions [18]. The extent to which these methodological constraints may have influenced the observed treatment effect remains uncertain, underscoring the need for an adequately powered trial using current diagnostic standards.

Elderly patients undergoing major gastrointestinal oncologic surgery are at relatively high risk for inadvertent perioperative hypothermia and associated cardiovascular complications. Age-related physiological decline impairs thermoregulatory vasoconstriction and metabolic heat production, an effect compounded by anesthetic-induced inhibition of the hypothalamic set-point [19,20]. In elderly patients undergoing laparoscopic colorectal procedures, the incidence of intraoperative hypothermia can reach 74% despite routine care [21]. Extensive surgical exposure, prolonged operative times, and the use of cold insufflation or irrigation fluids further accelerate heat dissipation [22,23]. However, clinical evidence reveal that only 20% of at-risk patients receive continuous temperature monitoring, and active warming measures remain markedly underutilized outside of rescue scenarios.

This trial employs an intelligent closed-loop thermoregulation system that could potentially addresses these shortcomings. By utilizing continuous tympanic membrane thermometry integrated with an automated warming device, the system maintains core temperature within a predefined normothermic window (target 36.8 °C) with a precision of 0.1 °C. This approach circumvents the physiological lag of rectal probes and the reactive nature of conventional forced-air warming triggered only at hypothermic thresholds [24,25]. A target set point of 36.8 °C was selected because we reasoned that even with closed-loop feedback control, core temperature would fluctuate around the programmed target owing to the inherent latency of physiological thermoregulatory responses and dynamic adjustment of device power output. This target aims to ensure that intraoperative core temperature remains above the guideline-recommended threshold of 36.0 °C.

We hypothesize that this proactive, precision-based thermoregulatory strategy will confer a clinically meaningful cardioprotective benefit. The present trial is designed to evaluate whether an intelligent closed-loop warming strategy is superior to routine thermal management in reducing the incidence of MINS in elderly patients undergoing gastrointestinal tumor resection [26,27].

Explanation for choice of comparator

The comparator arm employs routine thermal management consistent with current pragmatic clinical practice. This strategy consists of initial passive insulation, with active warming reserved as a rescue intervention triggered only when core temperature declines to ≤ 35.5 °C. This comparator was selected to determine whether a prophylactic, targeted normothermia strategy (maintaining core temperature near 37.0 °C) provides incremental clinical benefit over the reactive, threshold-based approach commonly employed in contemporary operating rooms.

Objectives and hypotheses

Primary objective

The primary objective of this trial is to evaluate the superiority of an intelligent, closed-loop thermoregulation strategy compared to routine thermal management in reducing the incidence of Myocardial Injury after Noncardiac Surgery (MINS) in elderly patients undergoing elective gastrointestinal tumor resection.

Exploratory objective

Furthermore, leveraging the high-resolution continuous temperature data acquired by the closed-loop system, an exploratory objective is to delineate the exposure-response relationship between intraoperative hypothermia duration and MINS. Specifically, we aim to identify a clinically actionable threshold of cumulative hypothermic exposure below which the risk of postoperative myocardial injury is not substantially increased. Such a threshold, if identified, could inform individualized, precision-based perioperative thermal management targets for the geriatric surgical population.

Statistical hypotheses for the primary outcome

The study is designed as a superiority trial. The prespecified superiority margin (Δ) is set at −2 percentage points for the absolute risk difference in MINS incidence. This margin represents the minimum clinically important difference, determined after consultation with clinical experts in perioperative medicine and cardiology. Given the strong prognostic association between MINS and 30-day mortality, a reduction in MINS incidence smaller than 2 percentage points is considered clinically negligible and unlikely to justify a change in perioperative temperature management practices. The formal statistical hypotheses are: Null Hypothesis (H0): P1 - P2 ≥ −2%;

The incidence of MINS in the intelligent thermoregulation group minus the incidence in the routine management group is greater than or equal to −2% (the intelligent strategy does not confer a clinically meaningful reduction). Alternative Hypothesis (H1): P1 - P2 < −2%;

The incidence of MINS in the intelligent thermoregulation group is more than 2 absolute percentage points lower than that in the routine management group.

Consistent with the sample size calculation (one-sided α = 0.05), superiority will be assessed using a one-sided test at the 0.05 significance level. Results will be reported using the two-sided 90% confidence interval for the between-group difference in proportions. Superiority will be declared if the upper bound of the two-sided 90% CI lies entirely below −2 percentage points.

Methods: patient and public involvement, trial design

Patient and public involvement

Patients or the public were not involved in the design of this protocol. The trial design was developed by the investigators and sponsor based on clinical equipoise and logistical feasibility. The results of this trial will be disseminated to participants upon request and through peer-reviewed publication.

Trial design

This is a prospective, multicenter, parallel-group, randomized controlled superiority trial with a 1:1 allocation ratio.

Methods: participants, interventions, and outcomes

Trial setting

The trial will be conducted across seven tertiary academic hospitals in China. The Third Xiangya Hospital of Central South University serves as both the coordinating center and the sponsor-investigator site for this trial. Participating sites include: Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences; Huadong Hospital Affiliated to Fudan University; Henan Cancer Hospital; Hunan Cancer Hospital; Hunan Provincial People’s Hospital; and The First Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University.

Eligibility criteria for participants

Inclusion Criteria: Age ≥ 65 years.

Scheduled for elective gastrointestinal tumor resection under general anesthesia.

Expected duration of surgery > 2 hours.

Provision of written informed consent.

Exclusion Criteria: Known allergy to device materials.

American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status ≥ IV.

Altered mental status or inability to cooperate with study procedures.

Less than 50% body surface area available for active warming.

Moderate to severe obesity (Body Mass Index ≥ 30 kg/m2).

Preoperative core temperature (tympanic temperature) > 37.5 °C.

Pre-existing diagnosis of thyroid dysfunction (hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism).

Severe liver dysfunction (Child-Pugh Class C).

Intracranial pathology potentially affecting thermoregulation.

Preoperative severe anemia (Hemoglobin < 60 g/L).

Any condition deemed unsuitable for participation by the investigator.

Eligibility criteria for sites and providers

All participating sites must be tertiary hospitals with the capacity for major abdominal oncologic surgery and standard operating room equipment for invasive monitoring. Anesthesia providers and surgeons are not required to meet specific credentialing criteria beyond their standard institutional privileges.

Intervention and comparator details

General Environment: Ambient operating room temperature will be maintained between 20 and 23 °C in both groups.

Temperature Monitoring: All participants will have a tympanic membrane temperature probe (WMT104, Beijing Weimai Intelligent Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.) placed for continuous core temperature monitoring from operating room entry until PACU discharge. Control Group (Routine Thermal Management): Participants will receive passive insulation (cotton blankets). Active warming (forced-air warming, fluid warmers, etc.) will be initiated only if core temperature decreases to ≤ 35.5 °C. The upper limit for any warming is 37.0 °C.

Intervention Group (Intelligent Thermoregulation): Participants will receive proactive, automated warming via a closed-loop system. Based on real-time feedback from the tympanic sensor, the warming device will dynamically adjust output to maintain a target temperature of 36.8 °C, with an upper limit of 37.0 °C.

Criteria for discontinuing or modifying interventions

The allocated thermal management strategy may be modified or discontinued if any of the following occur: Serious Adverse Event (SAE): If continuation of the allocated warming strategy is deemed by the attending anesthesiologist or principal investigator to pose an unacceptable risk to the participant’s safety, the intervention may be modified or discontinued.

Prolonged Intraoperative Hypotension: If cumulative intraoperative hypotension exceeds 30 minutes (defined as SBP <90 mmHg, MAP <60 mmHg, or a decrease >20% from baseline SBP or MAP [28]), the investigator should reassess hemodynamic management and may adjust the warming strategy if clinically indicated. Prolonged hypotension will be recorded as a major protocol deviation and will be addressed in a prespecified sensitivity analysis (see Section ‘Additional analyses’). However, participants with prolonged hypotension will not be withdrawn from the trial or excluded from the primary analysis for this reason alone.

Major Protocol Violation (other than hypotension): If a major protocol violation is identified, the violation will be recorded and the participant may be excluded from the per-protocol analysis. The participant will remain in the trial and be included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis whenever outcome data are available.

All randomized participants will be included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis according to their assigned group, regardless of whether the allocated intervention is modified or discontinued, provided that primary outcome data can be ascertained. Discontinuation or modification of the intervention does not constitute withdrawal from the trial or exclusion from the primary analysis.

Strategies to improve adherence

Adherence to the allocated thermal management strategy will be monitored through continuous electronic logging of the warming device settings and core temperature data. Anesthesia providers at each site will receive standardized in-service training on the protocol prior to local trial initiation.

Concomitant care

Permitted and recommended practices

Standard general anesthesia practices are permitted. Investigators may use adjunctive regional or local blocks at their discretion. To minimize inter-center variability while maintaining real-world applicability, the following principle-based recommendations are provided: Fluid management: Each center follows its established enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) or goal-directed therapy (GDT) protocol. The type and volume of fluids administered (crystalloids, colloids) are recorded in the eCRF.

Transfusion: A restrictive transfusion strategy is recommended. Red blood cell transfusion is suggested when hemoglobin falls below 70 g/L, or when hemoglobin is between 70 and 80 g/L with signs of inadequate oxygen delivery. All transfusions are recorded in detail.

Vasopressors: Intraoperative blood pressure is maintained within ±20% of the patient’s baseline value. The choice of vasopressor agent is left to the treating anesthesiologist; type, dose, and duration are recorded in the eCRF.

Analgesia: Multimodal analgesia is encouraged according to institutional pathways. All analgesic agents and doses are recorded in the eCRF.

Prohibited practices

The use of dexmedetomidine, esketamine, and neuraxial anesthesia is prohibited due to their potential confounding effects on postoperative shivering and thermoregulation.

Hemodynamic management

To minimize confounding from hypotension on MINS, the protocol stipulates maintenance of blood pressure within ±20% of the patient’s baseline value. Vasopressor use is not restricted but must be meticulously documented in the eCRF.

Outcomes

Primary outcome

Incidence of Myocardial Injury after Noncardiac Surgery (MINS) within the first 2 postoperative days. MINS is defined by postoperative troponin elevation adjudicated as resulting from myocardial ischemia without evidence of a non-ischemic etiology [26] (e.g. sepsis, rapid atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism et al.).

Measurement Variable: High-sensitivity Cardiac Troponin T (hs-cTnT) or Troponin I (hs-cTnI).

Time Point: Blood samples collected at baseline, Postoperative Day 1 (18 ± 6h), and Postoperative Day 2 (42 ± 6h).

Thresholds for Diagnosis: Based on assay type as specified by the American Heart Association [5]: hs-cTnT: ≥ 65 ng/L, OR 20 to < 65 ng/L with an absolute change of ≥ 5 ng/L from baseline.

hs-cTnI (Abbott): ≥ 75 ng/L.

hs-cTnI (Siemens): ≥ 60 ng/L.

Conventional TnI: ≥ Upper Reference Limit (URL) 99th percentile × 2.

Elevated Baseline: For patients with preoperative values > 80% of the above thresholds, a postoperative increase ≥ 20% is required.

Secondary outcomes

Surgical site infection (SSI)

Incidence of superficial incisional, deep incisional, or organ/space SSI from completion of the index operation until hospital discharge, adjudicated using the full CDC/NHSN criterion set (Patient Safety Component Manual, Chapter 9: Surgical Site Infection Event, January 2026).

Transfusion requirement

Administration of any allogeneic blood component (packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate) from the start of surgery through the index hospitalization. Autologous cell-salvaged blood is excluded. Both the proportion of participants transfused and the amount transfused will be recorded.

Hypothermia burden

Cumulative area below the 36.0 °C threshold from operating-room entry to PACU discharge. The total duration of hypothermia will also be reported.

Emergence delirium

Incidence assessed at 30 min after tracheal extubation using the CAM-ICU.

Delayed emergence

Inability to follow a simple verbal command persisting for >60 min after discontinuation of all general anesthetic agents.

Postoperative shivering

Incidence of clinically relevant shivering during PACU stay. Assessment at PACU admission, 15 min, and 30 min, and the highest score recorded will be used for analysis.

Complete operational definitions, including diagnostic criteria, threshold values, and assessment protocols for all the secondary outcomes, are provided in Table S1.

Harms

Adverse Events (AEs) and Serious Adverse Events (SAEs) will be assessed systematically from the initiation of intervention through the 3-year follow-up period. All events will be recorded in the electronic Case Report Form (eCRF). Causality assessment related to the device or study procedures will be performed by the site investigator.

Methods: sample size and recruitment

Sample size

The sample size calculation is based on the superiority hypothesis for the primary outcome (MINS). Assuming a control group MINS incidence of 12% in this elderly population [27] and an anticipated reduction to 6% in the intervention group (absolute risk difference of −6 percentage points), with a prespecified superiority margin (Δ) of −2 percentage points, a one-sided significance level of 0.05, and a power of 80%, a total of 1,262 participants (631 per group) is required. This calculation was performed using PASS software (Version: 25.0.6). To account for an anticipated dropout rate of 10%, the target enrollment is set at 1,390 participants (695 per group).

Recruitment

Participants will be identified through pre-admission testing clinics and elective surgical schedules at the seven participating centers. Enrollment will be competitive across sites to ensure timely completion.

Methods: assignment of interventions

Sequence generation

The random allocation sequence will be generated by an independent biostatistician not involved in trial execution using the SAS software (Version 9.4).

Type of randomization

A stratified, permuted-block randomization method will be employed. Randomization will be stratified by study site to ensure balance within each center. Block sizes will be concealed and documented in a separate document unavailable to the enrollment personnel.

Allocation concealment mechanism

Concealment of the allocation sequence will be maintained through a central, secure Interactive Web Response System (IWRS). The sequence is not accessible to site staff prior to participant registration.

Implementation

Eligible participants will be registered in the IWRS by authorized site personnel. The system will assign a unique randomization number and the corresponding group allocation (1:1) only after baseline information is confirmed. Personnel enrolling participants will have no access to the underlying sequence generation algorithm or future assignments.

Blinding

Due to the nature of the intervention (visible use of active warming equipment), blinding of participants and intraoperative anesthesia providers is not feasible. However, the following parties will be blinded: Outcome Assessors Investigators adjudicating MINS events and SSI diagnoses will be blinded to group allocation.

Data Analysts The statistical team will perform primary analyses using masked group identifiers (Group A vs. Group B).

Unblinding procedures

Because the clinical care team is not masked to treatment assignment, formal unblinding procedures do not apply to these personnel. The statisticians performing the primary analyses will remain masked to group allocation until database lock. Emergency unblinding of these statisticians is not anticipated but may be undertaken in exceptional circumstances if deemed necessary by the independent safety monitor or the Ethics Committee to investigate a potential safety signal. Any such unmasking must be approved by the Steering Committee and will be fully documented, including the rationale, date, and individuals involved.

Methods: data collection, management, and analysis

Data collection methods

Data will be collected prospectively using a validated electronic Case Report Form (eCRF) system. Physiological Data: The intraoperative temperature and hemodynamic data will be captured directly from the monitors and exported as .CSV files for direct import into the study database to minimize transcription errors.

Laboratory Data: Local laboratory reference ranges and assay platforms (hs-cTnT/I) will be documented.

Instrument Validity: The QoR-15 scale and Shivering Scale are validated instruments in perioperative research.

Participant retention and follow-up

  Follow-up at 30 days will be conducted via telephone if the patient is discharged.

Long-term survival follow-up (6–36 months) will be conducted via telephone interviews or review of national death registry data every 6 months.

For participants who discontinue the intervention early, consent will be sought to continue collection of primary outcome data (MINS).

Data management

Data management will utilize EpiData (version 4.6.0) software. Procedures include: Double Data Verification: Discrepancy queries generated by Clinical Research Associates (CRAs) will be resolved against source documentation.

Data Entry: Electronic data capture with built-in range checks and logic validation.

Storage: Data will be stored on secure, password-protected servers with regular backups. Only authorized study personnel will have access.

Statistical methods

Primary Outcome Analysis: The primary analysis will employ the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test, stratified by study center, to compare the proportion of participants with MINS between groups. Consistent with the sample size calculation, superiority will be tested at a one-sided significance level of 0.05. For clarity of presentation, the between-group difference in MINS incidence will be reported with its two-sided 90% confidence interval, the upper bound of which corresponds to the one-sided 95% upper confidence limit. Superiority will be declared if the upper bound of the two-sided 90% CI lies entirely below the prespecified margin of −2 percentage points.

Secondary Outcomes Analysis: Continuous variables will be analyzed using independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests as appropriate. Categorical variables will be analyzed using chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests. Repeated measures will be analyzed using mixed-effects models.

Analysis populations

Intention-to-Treat (ITT)/Full Analysis Set (FAS): All randomized participants, analyzed according to the group to which they were assigned. This is the primary analysis set.

Per-Protocol Set (PPS): A subset of FAS excluding participants with major protocol violations. This will serve as a sensitivity analysis.

Safety Analysis Set (SAS): All participants who received any trial intervention, analyzed according to the treatment actually received.

Missing data

For the primary outcome, missing data will be handled using a conservative approach. Sensitivity analyses will be performed using multiple imputation and worst-case/best-case scenario imputation to assess the robustness of the findings. For secondary endpoints, the Last Observation Carried Forward (LOCF) method may be used where appropriate.

Additional analyses

Prespecified subgroup analyses for the primary outcome will explore the consistency of the treatment effect across the following subgroups, including: Surgical Approach (laparoscopic vs. open);

History of cardiovascular disease (present vs. absent);

Age category (65–74 vs. ≥75 years);

Duration of surgery (≤ median vs. > median);

Body mass index (< 24.0 vs. ≥ 24.0 kg/m2).

Subgroup analyses are exploratory; the trial is not powered for individual subgroup comparisons. Results will be displayed as forest plots, and interaction tests will be reported.

Sensitivity analyses will include: Per-protocol analysis excluding participants with major protocol violations;

As-treated analysis based on the thermal management strategy actually received;

Analysis excluding participants with cumulative intraoperative hypotension exceeding 30 minutes;

Multiple imputation for missing primary outcome data.

The classification of major versus minor protocol violations will be finalized at the data review meeting prior to database lock.

Methods: monitoring

Data Monitoring Committee

Given that both the investigational closed-loop warming system and the routine thermal management strategy evaluated in this trial employ legally marketed medical devices with established safety profiles, a formal independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) with predefined stopping rules is not mandated for this trial. However, a three-tiered safety and data monitoring framework has been established to ensure ongoing trial integrity and participant safety. The principal investigators (W.O. and Q.L.) will convene quarterly internal safety review meetings to audit adverse event rates, protocol compliance, and site performance metrics across all participating centers. Findings will be documented in written reports maintained at the coordinating center.

An independent safety monitor (a senior anesthesiologist not otherwise affiliated with the trial) has been appointed to review accumulating safety data at six-month intervals. The independent monitor will have access to unblinded group-level safety data and will report directly to the Ethics Committee of the coordinating center. Should any safety signal be identified, the monitor is empowered to recommend suspension or early termination of the trial to the Steering Committee and the Ethics Committee.

Additionally, if emerging data or external evidence indicates that a formal Data Monitoring Committee with predefined stopping boundaries is warranted, the Steering Committee will establish such a committee before further enrollment proceeds.

Interim analyses and stopping guidelines

No formal interim efficacy analyses are planned. The trial may be terminated early for safety concerns or futility based on the recommendation of the sponsor and lead principal investigator.

Trial monitoring

Site monitoring will be conducted by qualified CRAs according to Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines. Monitoring visits will include source data verification, review of regulatory files, and assessment of protocol compliance. The frequency of monitoring visits will be determined by site enrollment rate and data quality metrics.

Protocol adherence will be audited continuously through electronic logging of the allocated thermal management strategy and through regular monitoring visits. The coordinating center will generate quarterly site performance reports, including enrollment rate, protocol deviation rate, completeness of primary outcome data, and timeliness of data entry. These reports will be reviewed by the Steering Committee. Corrective and preventive actions will be implemented for centers with performance concerns, which may include additional training, targeted monitoring, or suspension of enrollment.

Ancillary studies

Confidentiality

Discussion

This multicenter, randomized controlled superiority trial is designed to address a persistent evidence gap in perioperative thermoregulation: whether proactive, precision-guided maintenance of normothermia reduces the incidence of Myocardial Injury after Noncardiac Surgery (MINS) in a high-risk geriatric surgical population.

The association between inadvertent perioperative hypothermia and adverse cardiovascular events has been recognized for decades. Observational studies demonstrate that hypothermic patients exhibit significantly elevated rates of postoperative myocardial ischemia and ventricular arrhythmias [12,13]. Despite this, the causal relationship between aggressive normothermia and cardioprotection remains inadequately established. A randomized trial by Frank et al. [12] suggested a reduction in morbid cardiac events with normothermia; however, the study enrolled only 300 patients and relied predominantly on Holter electrocardiography rather than contemporary high‑sensitivity troponin assays for event ascertainment, potentially missing the majority of true myocardial injury events [18]. The limited number of outcome events (fewer than ten) constrains statistical precision and precludes definitive clinical conclusions. Consequently, current practice guidelines recommend a core temperature target of ≥36.0 °C, a threshold that is arguably below the true physiological norm and may not represent the optimal target for myocardial protection [28].

The present trial overcomes these limitations through three key design features. First, it employs a sample size adequately powered to detect a clinically meaningful reduction in MINS, defined using high-sensitivity troponin thresholds endorsed by the American Heart Association [5]. Second, the continuous tympanic membrane thermometry integrated within the closed-loop system generates unprecedented granularity of intraoperative temperature data, enabling exploratory delineation of the exposure-response relationship between hypothermia duration and myocardial injury. Third, the prespecified superiority margin (Δ = −2 percentage points) defines the minimum between‑group difference considered clinically meaningful, against which the trial results will be assessed. This threshold was selected after consultation with perioperative medicine and cardiology experts: given the strong association between MINS and 30-day mortality, a reduction in MINS incidence smaller than 2 percentage points was judged unlikely to warrant a change in clinical practice. The margin is deliberately conservative relative to the anticipated 6-percentage-point effect, ensuring that any benefit detected by the trial is both clinically relevant and statistically robust.

Achieving the intended between-group temperature separation is critical to trial validity. Under routine care, unwarmed patients undergoing major abdominal surgery typically reach a final intraoperative core temperature near 35.5 °C, whereas the intervention group will be managed using the closed‑loop system with a target set point of 36.8 °C, around which core temperature is expected to fluctuate (upper limit: 37.0 °C). An average between‑group gradient of approximately 1 °C is therefore anticipated. A substantially smaller gradient would reduce the statistical power to detect outcome differences and could compromise the interpretability of the primary analysis. To optimize temperature separation, the intervention is applied proactively from the induction of anesthesia, and the control group receives active warming only as rescue therapy below 35.5 °C, thereby minimizing contamination from concurrent active warming.

Blinding of the intraoperative anesthesia team is not feasible because the active warming equipment used in the intervention arm is physically distinct from standard passive insulation. Nevertheless, the primary outcome (MINS) is a laboratory-based endpoint defined by prespecified troponin thresholds, which are inherently objective. Troponin concentrations will be adjudicated by an independent clinical events committee masked to group allocation. Secondary outcomes, including surgical site infection and transfusion requirements, will also be adjudicated by assessors blinded to treatment assignment. These measures are expected to substantially mitigate the risk of ascertainment bias arising from the open-label design. Additionally, intraoperative hypotension is a recognized competing risk factor for MINS. Although all randomized participants are retained in the primary intention-to-treat analysis, the observed relationship between hypothermia and myocardial injury may be partially confounded by hypotensive episodes. The prespecified sensitivity analysis excluding participants with prolonged hypotension is designed to assess the robustness of the primary findings to this potential confounding.

Elderly patients undergoing gastrointestinal tumor resection face a confluence of predisposing factors that place them at disproportionately high risk for both inadvertent perioperative hypothermia and postoperative cardiovascular complications. Should the intelligent thermoregulation strategy prove superior, the results would provide evidence to support a transition from reactive, threshold‑based warming to proactive, automated normothermia maintenance in this vulnerable cohort. An exploratory analysis of cumulative hypothermic exposure may further define a temperature‑time threshold below which the risk of MINS does not appear substantially elevated, thereby informing individualized, precision‑oriented perioperative thermal management. Conversely, a neutral result would undermine the assumption that mild intraoperative hypothermia is a clinically important causal contributor to myocardial injury and would provide a rationale for redirecting investigative efforts toward alternative modifiable risk factors [27].

Finally, a limitation of this trial should be acknowledged. The SAGE trial is an open-label design, because the active warming equipment is physically distinct from standard passive insulation, blinding of the intraoperative anesthesia team is not feasible. Although the primary outcome (MINS) is objective, the open-label design cannot fully exclude subtle behavioral differences in intraoperative care between groups.

In conclusion, this trial is designed to generate new evidence on the association between intraoperative hypothermia exposure and postoperative cardiovascular complications, with MINS as the primary endpoint, in elderly surgical patients. The trial will evaluate whether a closed‑loop, target‑driven thermoregulation strategy can reduce myocardial injury after gastrointestinal tumor resection by providing more comprehensive perioperative temperature protection. Furthermore, leveraging the large‑scale, high‑resolution continuous temperature data collected across multiple centers, this trial would explore and estimate a hypothermia exposure threshold that is closely associated with postoperative complications in geriatric patients, which could potentially contribute to individualized, evidence‑based perioperative temperature management for this high‑risk population.
